julia: How does Julia decide which method of a function to run for a call?
By the runtime types of all the arguments
By the type of the first argument only
By the order in which methods were defined
By the declared return type of each method
Julia uses multiple dispatch: the most specific method matching the types of every argument is chosen, not just the first one as in single-dispatch OOP.
In Julia, after f(x::Int) = 1 and f(x::Number) = 2, what does f(3.0) return?
A MethodError
3.0 is a Float64, which is a Number but not an Int, so the f(x::Number) method is the only match.
In Julia, after f(x::Int, y) = 1 and f(x, y::Int) = 2, what happens when you call f(1, 2)?
A MethodError saying the call is ambiguous
It returns 1, since the first argument wins
It returns 2, since the newest method wins
It returns whichever method was compiled first
Both methods match (Int, Int) equally well and neither is more specific, so Julia reports an ambiguity instead of guessing.
What does [1, 2, 3] .+ 1 return in Julia?
A MethodError
The dot makes + broadcast, so the scalar 1 is added to each element.
In Julia 1.x, what happens when you evaluate [1, 2, 3] + 1 (no dot)?
A MethodError, as + has no vector-scalar method
It returns [2, 3, 4] through implicit broadcasting
It returns [1, 2, 3, 1] by appending the value
It returns 7 by summing every element together
Julia does not broadcast implicitly; you must write [1, 2, 3] .+ 1 to add a scalar to every element.
What does the @. macro do in the Julia line @. y = 2x^2 + 1?
Turns every operator, call and assignment into its dotted form
Runs the whole right-hand side in parallel on all available threads
Marks the expression as type-stable for the compiler
Evaluates the expression once and caches the result
@. is shorthand for writing y .= 2 .* x .^ 2 .+ 1, so the whole expression fuses into one broadcast loop.
Why is the Julia function f(x) = x > 0 ? 1 : 1.0 considered a performance problem?
Its return type depends on a runtime value, so it is type-unstable
Ternary expressions cannot be compiled to native code by the JIT
Comparing an integer with 0 forces a slow conversion to BigInt
Float literals inside function bodies disable JIT compilation entirely
The result may be Int64 or Float64 depending on x, so callers cannot be specialized on a single concrete type.
Why do non-constant global variables used in hot loops slow Julia code down?
The compiler cannot assume their type, which may change at any time
Globals are reloaded from disk on every single access in the loop
Globals are deep-copied into each iteration of the loop body
Globals disable broadcasting and SIMD inside every loop that uses them
Code touching an untyped global must handle any type, so it cannot be specialized. Pass values as function arguments or declare them const.
Why is the first call of a Julia function in a new session often much slower than later calls?
The method is compiled to native code for those argument types
The first call is interpreted and its result is cached for later
Packages are downloaded during the first call
The garbage collector runs a full sweep before it
Julia compiles a specialized method the first time it sees a combination of argument types; later calls reuse that native code.
What is the main use of the @code_warntype macro in Julia?
Showing inferred types and highlighting type instability
Printing the native assembly code generated for a method
Listing all warnings emitted by the parser for a file
Checking that a package has no deprecated function calls
@code_warntype shows the types the compiler inferred and marks abstract types such as Any. @code_native is the one that prints assembly.
What does a Julia macro receive as its input?
The unevaluated expressions of its arguments
The evaluated values of its arguments
The compiled native machine code of its arguments
Only string literals passed to it
Macros run when code is expanded, before evaluation; they take Expr and Symbol objects and return a new expression to be compiled.
What does typeof(:(a + b)) return in Julia?
Expr
Symbol
Function
Int64
Quoting a compound expression produces an Expr object. Quoting a single name, as in :a, produces a Symbol.
How do you start Julia 1.5 or later with 4 threads available to Threads.@threads?
julia --threads 4
julia --procs 4
julia --cores 4
julia --workers 4
--threads (or -t) sets the number of threads. --procs (or -p) starts extra worker processes for Distributed, which is a different model.
In Julia with several threads, what is the risk of s = 0; Threads.@threads for i in 1:1000 s += i end?
A data race can make the final sum wrong
Julia rejects the loop at compile time
The loop silently runs on one thread only
Each thread gets a private s that is summed at the end
Threads read and write s concurrently without synchronization. Use atomics, a lock, or per-thread partial sums instead.
Which Julia tool splits a loop across separate worker processes rather than threads?
@distributed from the Distributed standard library
Threads.@spawn from the Base.Threads module
@simd from Base for vectorized loops
@inbounds from Base for faster indexing
@distributed runs loop iterations on worker processes started with addprocs or julia -p. Threads.@spawn uses threads in one process.
For a square matrix A and vector b in Julia, what does A \ b compute?
The solution x of the linear system A * x = b
The elementwise division of b by each entry of A
The inverse of A multiplied by itself
The left bit shift of A by b positions
The backslash operator solves linear systems with an appropriate factorization, which is faster and more accurate than inv(A) * b.
For a complex matrix A in Julia, what does A' return?
The adjoint (conjugate transpose) of A
The plain transpose of A, without conjugation
The determinant of A as a scalar
A flattened into a column vector
A' is adjoint(A), which conjugates complex entries. Use transpose(A) when you need a transpose without conjugation.
In the Julia REPL, which key switches into Pkg mode?
] enters Pkg mode for commands like add and status. ? opens help mode and ; opens shell mode.
In a Julia project, which file records the exact versions of every dependency, including indirect ones?
Manifest.toml
Project.toml
Package.toml
Julia.toml
Project.toml lists direct dependencies and compatibility bounds; Manifest.toml pins the full resolved dependency graph for reproducibility.
Julia arrays are column-major. For a large matrix A, which nested loop order is usually faster when visiting A[i, j]?
The inner loop runs over the first index i
The inner loop runs over the second index j
Both orders give identical memory access speed
The outer loop must run over both indices
Elements of a column are adjacent in memory, so varying i in the inner loop gives sequential, cache-friendly access.
r-lang: What does c(1, 2, 3) * 2 return in R?
An error
Arithmetic in R is vectorized, so the multiplication applies to every element.
What does c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20) return in R?
11 22 NA NA
A length error
R recycles the shorter vector, so it becomes 10 20 10 20. A warning appears only when the longer length is not a multiple of the shorter.
Why is sum(x) on a large numeric vector usually much faster than summing with an explicit R for loop?
sum() runs one compiled loop in C over the whole vector
sum() spreads the work over all available CPU cores
sum() caches results from earlier calls on the same vector
for loops in R copy the vector on each pass
Vectorized built-ins do the loop in compiled code, avoiding the per-iteration interpreter overhead of an R-level loop.
What does mean(c(1, NA, 3)) return in R?
NA
An error
Missing values propagate through most calculations. Use na.rm = TRUE to ignore them.
What does mean(c(1, NA, 3), na.rm = TRUE) return in R?
NA
na.rm = TRUE drops the NA, leaving the mean of 1 and 3.
What does NA == NA return in R?
NA
TRUE
FALSE
An error
Comparing an unknown value with another unknown value gives an unknown result, so the comparison returns NA.
Which R expression correctly tests which elements of x are missing?
is.na(x)
x == NA
is.null(x)
missing(x)
is.na() returns TRUE for each missing element. x == NA returns all NA, is.null() checks for NULL, and missing() checks function arguments.
For a tibble tb with several columns, what does tb[, 1] return?
A tibble with one column
An atomic vector of the first column
The first row as a tibble
An error about missing row indices
Tibbles never drop to a vector with [. A base data.frame returns a vector for df[, 1]; use tb[[1]] or tb$name to get the vector from a tibble.
With dplyr, what does df %>% filter(age > 30) do?
Keeps only the rows where age is greater than 30
Keeps only the columns whose names contain age
Sorts the rows by age in descending order
Adds a new logical column named age > 30
filter() selects rows by a condition. select() picks columns, arrange() sorts and mutate() adds columns.
Which dplyr verb adds a new column computed from existing columns?
mutate()
summarise()
select()
arrange()
mutate() keeps all rows and adds or modifies columns. summarise() collapses groups into single rows.
What does df %>% group_by(team) %>% summarise(n = n()) return?
One row per team with the number of rows in it
The original rows with a new count column
A single row with the number of teams
The rows of df sorted by team name
summarise() collapses each group to one row, and n() counts the rows in the current group.
In ggplot(df, aes(x = height, y = weight)) + geom_point(), what does aes() define?
How data columns map to visual properties
The color theme applied to the plot
The size of the saved image file
Which rows of df are drawn
Aesthetic mappings link variables to properties such as position, color and size. geom_point() then draws them as points.
In R S3, how does print(obj) end up calling print.myclass?
UseMethod() dispatches on the object's class attribute
setMethod() dispatches on formal slot definitions
R matches the variable name against method names
R6 inheritance resolves the method at runtime
print is an S3 generic that calls UseMethod("print"), which looks up print.<class> for each class in class(obj), then print.default.
Which function defines a formal S4 class in R?
setClass()
UseMethod()
structure()
R6Class()
setClass() declares an S4 class with typed slots. structure() only sets attributes (used for S3), and R6Class() comes from the R6 package.
What is the type of the result of lapply(1:3, function(x) x * 2) in R?
A list of length 3
A numeric vector of length 3
A 3 by 1 numeric matrix
A data frame with 3 rows
lapply() always returns a list. sapply() would simplify this result to the numeric vector 2 4 6.
For a numeric matrix m, what does apply(m, 1, sum) return in R?
The sum of each row
The sum of each column
The sum of all elements
The cumulative sum of row 1
MARGIN = 1 applies the function over rows; MARGIN = 2 would apply it over columns.
Which R call downloads and installs the dplyr package from CRAN?
install.packages("dplyr")
library("dplyr")
download.packages("dplyr")
require("dplyr")
install.packages() fetches the package from CRAN and installs it. download.packages() only saves the source files, while library() and require() only attach a package that is already installed.
Which R call fits a logistic regression of a binary outcome y on x?
glm(y ~ x, family = binomial, data = df)
lm(y ~ x, family = binomial, data = df)
glm(y ~ x, family = poisson, data = df)
glm(y ~ x, family = gaussian, data = df)
Logistic regression is a GLM with the binomial family and logit link. lm() has no family argument, and poisson is for counts.
In R, what does g() return after x <- 1; g <- function() { x <- 2; h <- function() x; h() }?
The value 2
The value 1
The value NULL
An error: x not found
R uses lexical scoping: h looks up x in the environment where h was defined, which is inside g, where x is 2.
In R, what is x after x <- 0; f <- function() x <<- x + 1; f(); f()?
NA
<<- assigns in the enclosing environments, here the global one, so each call increments the global x. With <- the global x would stay 0.
matlab: In MATLAB, with A = [1 2; 3 4], what does A .* A return?
.* multiplies element by element. [7 10; 15 22] is the matrix product A * A.
In MATLAB, with A = [1 2; 3 4], what does A * A return?
* is matrix multiplication: for example the top left entry is 1*1 + 2*3 = 7.
In MATLAB, with v = [10 20 30], what does v(end) return?
end inside an index means the last position. MATLAB indexing starts at 1.
In MATLAB, with A = [1 2; 3 4], what does A(:)' return?
A(:) stacks all elements into a column in column-major order (down each column), and ' turns it into a row.
In MATLAB, with x = [1 2 3], what happens when you evaluate x^2?
An error, since x^2 needs a square matrix
It returns [1 4 9], squaring each element
It returns 14, the dot product of x with x
It returns [2 4 6], doubling each element
^ means matrix power. Use the elementwise operator x.^2 to get [1 4 9].
In MATLAB, with x = [3 -1 4 -2], what does x(x > 0) return?
x > 0 creates a logical mask, and indexing with it keeps only the elements where the mask is true. [1 3] would come from find(x > 0).
In MATLAB, with c = {1, 'abc'}, what does class(c(2)) return?
'cell'
'char'
'string'
'double'
Parentheses on a cell array return a smaller cell array. Curly braces, c{2}, return the contents, which is the char array 'abc'.
Which MATLAB statement creates a structure with a field age equal to 20?
s = struct('age', 20)
s = cell('age', 20)
struct takes field name and value pairs. The curly braces version creates a cell array, not a structure.
What is the key difference between a MATLAB script file and a function file?
A function has its own workspace; a script uses the caller's
A script cannot contain loops or if blocks, only statements
A function cannot call any other function or a script
A script must start with the function keyword on its first line
Variables created by a script appear in the base (or calling) workspace, while a function's variables are local unless returned.
A MATLAB file's first line is function y = area(r). What should the file be named?
area.m
y.m
r.m
function.m
The file name should match the name of the first function so MATLAB can find it; if they differ, MATLAB uses the file name.
Which MATLAB command keeps the current plot so the next plot command draws on the same axes?
hold on
figure
grid on
axis on
hold on retains existing graphics. figure opens a new window, and grid on only adds grid lines.
In MATLAB, what does plot(x, y, 'r--') draw?
A red dashed line
A red dotted line
Red circle markers
A red solid line
In the line spec, r is red and -- is dashed. A dotted line is ':' and circle markers are 'o'.
In Simulink, what does a continuous Integrator block (shown as 1/s) output?
The integral of its input signal over time
The derivative of its input signal over time
The running average of its input signal
The input multiplied by a constant gain
1/s is the Laplace-domain form of integration. A Derivative block computes du/dt and a Gain block multiplies by a constant.
Which Simulink block is commonly used to view a signal plotted against simulation time?
Scope
Gain
Constant
Sum
The Scope block displays signals over time during simulation. Gain, Constant and Sum are math and source blocks.
Which MATLAB function reads a CSV file with a header row into a table?
readtable
fopen
textscan
load
readtable detects the header and column types and returns a table. fopen only opens a file handle, textscan returns a cell array, and load reads MAT files or plain numeric text.
In MATLAB, what does fid = fopen('missing.txt', 'r') set fid to when the file does not exist?
NaN
fopen returns -1 on failure rather than throwing, so check fid before reading. The optional second output gives the error message.
Why is x = A \ b usually preferred over x = inv(A) * b in MATLAB?
It solves the system directly, faster and more accurately
It works only for diagonal and triangular matrices
It returns the inverse of A as a side effect
It avoids the need for b to be a column vector with matching rows
Backslash picks a suitable factorization and never forms the inverse, which costs more and amplifies rounding errors.
In MATLAB, what do V and D contain after [V, D] = eig(A)?
V holds eigenvectors as columns, D the eigenvalues on its diagonal
V holds eigenvalues as a vector, D the eigenvectors as rows
V is the inverse of A and D holds its determinant on the diagonal
V holds singular values as columns, D the rank of A on its diagonal
eig returns matrices satisfying A*V = V*D. Singular values come from svd, not eig.
Which MATLAB function minimizes a multivariable function without derivatives, using the Nelder-Mead simplex method?
fminsearch
fminbnd
lsqnonlin
fzero
fminsearch is derivative-free and unconstrained. fzero finds roots of a one-variable function, fminbnd minimizes one variable on an interval, and lsqnonlin solves nonlinear least squares.
Which MATLAB command makes execution pause at the line where an error occurs, so you can inspect variables?
dbstop if error
dbcont
dbquit
dbclear if error
dbstop if error enters debug mode at the failing line. dbclear if error removes that breakpoint, dbcont resumes execution and dbquit exits debug mode.
haskell: What does take 3 [1..] evaluate to in Haskell?
An infinite loop
A type error
Lazy evaluation means [1..] is only produced as far as take needs, so the infinite list is never fully built.
In Haskell, what does length [1, 2, undefined] return?
The value 3
The value 2
An exception
No result, it loops
length only counts list cells and never evaluates the elements, so the undefined element is not forced.
What does referential transparency mean in Haskell?
An expression can be replaced by its value without changing behavior
Every variable can be reassigned only once within its enclosing scope
All functions must declare their argument and result types explicitly
References to data are shared and visible to all running threads
Pure functions always give the same result for the same input and have no side effects, so substitution is always safe.
Why does getLine have the type IO String rather than String in Haskell?
Reading input is a side effect, so it is tracked by the IO type
Strings in Haskell are always lazy IO streams read from stdin
String values are not allowed in pure code, only inside IO
IO makes the function run faster when it reads large or streamed input
IO marks actions that interact with the world, keeping pure functions free of effects and preserving referential transparency.
In Haskell, what does the constraint in elem :: Eq a => a -> [a] -> Bool require?
The type a must have an Eq instance
The list must contain at least one element
The type a must be a numeric type
Both arguments must be the same value
Eq a is a type class constraint: elem needs == to compare elements, so it works for any type with an Eq instance.
What does deriving (Show, Eq) do in data Color = Red | Green deriving (Show, Eq)?
Generates Show and Eq instances for Color automatically
Makes Color a subclass of both the Show and Eq classes
Converts Red and Green into strings at compile time
Exports Color and its constructors from the current module
The compiler writes standard instances, so show Red gives "Red" and Red == Green works.
Given data Shape = Circle Double | Rect Double Double in Haskell, what is the type of Rect?
Double -> Double -> Shape
Shape -> Double -> Double
(Double, Double) -> Shape
Double -> Shape
Data constructors are functions: Rect takes two Doubles and returns a Shape.
In Haskell, what does fmap (+1) Nothing return?
Nothing
Just 1
Just 0
An error
The Maybe functor applies the function only inside Just. Nothing stays Nothing.
In Haskell, what does Left "err" >>= (\x -> Right (x + 1)) return?
Left "err"
Right ("err" + 1)
Right 1
A runtime error
For Either, >>= short-circuits on Left: the function is never called and the error is passed through.
In Haskell, what does do { x <- Just 3; y <- Nothing; return (x + y) } evaluate to?
Nothing
Just 3
Just Nothing
A type error
In the Maybe monad, any Nothing in the chain makes the whole computation Nothing.
In Haskell, what does (+) <$> Just 3 <*> Just 4 return?
Just 7
Just (Just 7)
Nothing
<$> maps (+) into Just, giving Just (3 +), and <*> applies that wrapped function to Just 4.
In Haskell, what does fmap (+1) (1, 2) return?
A type error
The Functor instance for pairs maps only over the second component, because the first type is fixed in the instance.
In Haskell, with f [] = 0 and f (x:_) = x, what does f [7, 8, 9] return?
The pattern (x:_) matches a non-empty list, binding its head to x and ignoring the tail.
A Haskell function has only the equation g (Just x) = x. What happens when g Nothing is evaluated?
A runtime exception for non-exhaustive patterns
It returns Nothing, passing the input through
It returns the default value for the type of x
It returns undefined lazily without ever failing
GHC compiles incomplete patterns (it may warn) and throws an exception when no equation matches at runtime.
In Haskell, given add :: Int -> Int -> Int, what is the type of add 2?
Int -> Int
Int -> Int -> Int
(Int, Int) -> Int
A type error
Functions are curried, so applying one argument returns a function waiting for the rest.
Why does map (-1) [5, 6] fail to type-check in Haskell, while map (subtract 1) [5, 6] works?
(-1) is parsed as the number negative one, not a section
Negative numbers cannot appear inside lists
map only accepts functions of two arguments
subtract is a special macro that GHC expands at compile time
Haskell treats (-1) as a literal, so map gets a number instead of a function. subtract 1 (or (\x -> x - 1)) gives [4, 5].
In Haskell, after let xs = [1, 2, 3]; ys = 0 : xs, which statement is true?
xs is unchanged and ys shares its cells
xs becomes [0, 1, 2, 3] as well
ys holds a full deep copy of xs
The code fails because xs is immutable
Values are immutable, so cons builds a new cell pointing at the existing list. Sharing is safe because nothing can mutate xs.
What is the type of the bind operator (>>=) in Haskell?
Monad m => m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b
Monad m => (a -> b) -> m a -> m b
Monad m => m a -> (a -> b) -> m b
Monad m => (a -> m b) -> m a -> m b
Bind feeds the result of a monadic value into a function that returns a new monadic value. The other types belong to fmap, a flipped fmap, and =<< (bind with its arguments flipped).
In Haskell, what does foldr (\x acc -> x || acc) False (repeat True) return?
It returns True
It returns False
It never terminates
A stack overflow
|| is lazy in its second argument, and foldr passes the rest of the fold lazily, so the first True ends the computation.
What is the usual type of main in a Haskell program?
IO ()
String
Maybe ()
main is an IO action run by the runtime system; () means it produces no meaningful result.
ocaml: What type does OCaml infer for let f x = x + 1?
int -> int
float -> float
int -> int -> int
+ works only on ints in OCaml, so Hindley-Milner inference fixes both x and the result to int.
What type does OCaml infer for let id x = x?
int -> int
unit -> unit
Nothing constrains x, so inference generalizes it to a type variable. 'a -> 'b would claim it can return any type, which is false.
What type does OCaml infer for let f x y = x +. y?
float -> float -> float
int -> int -> int
(float * float) -> float
+. is float addition, so both arguments and the result are float, and the function is curried.
What happens when OCaml compiles the expression 1 + 2.0?
A type error, since + expects int and 2.0 is a float
It evaluates to 3.0 by converting 1 to float
It evaluates to 3 by truncating 2.0
It compiles but raises an exception at runtime
OCaml has no implicit numeric conversion. Use 1.0 +. 2.0 or float_of_int 1 +. 2.0.
In the OCaml 4.06 or later toplevel, what type is reported for let r = ref []?
'_weak1 list ref
'a list ref
'a. 'a list ref
int list ref
The value restriction stops generalizing ref [], so it gets a weak type variable that becomes fixed on first use.
In OCaml, what does match [1; 2; 3] with [] -> 0 | x :: _ -> x evaluate to?
x :: _ matches a non-empty list, binding the head to x and ignoring the tail.
In OCaml, let f = function Some x -> x has no None case. What does the compiler do?
Warns the match is not exhaustive; f None raises Match_failure
Refuses to compile the function until a None case is added
Adds a default case that returns None for missing input
Infers that f only accepts values of type int option, and compiles
Non-exhaustive matches produce a warning (warning 8) with an example of an unmatched value, and fail at runtime if it occurs.
Given type shape = Circle of float | Square of float in OCaml, which expression builds a circle of radius 2?
Circle 2.0
Circle 2
new Circle 2.0
Circle.make 2.0
Constructors are applied directly to their argument. Circle 2 is a type error because 2 is an int.
What does an OCaml module signature (sig ... end) specify?
The types and values that a module exposes
The runtime order in which modules load
The compiler flags used to build a module
The memory layout of a module's values
A signature is a module's interface. Items left out of the signature are hidden, and types can be made abstract.
What is a functor in OCaml?
A module that is parameterized by another module
A type that supports a map operation
A function that returns another function
A record whose fields are all functions
Functors are functions from modules to modules, such as Map.Make, which takes an ordered type and returns a map module.
Which OCaml line creates a map module keyed by strings?
module SMap = Map.Make(String)
let SMap = Map.create String
module SMap = new Map(String)
type SMap = Map.Make String
Map.Make is a functor applied to a module with type t and compare; String provides both.
Why can let rec sum = function [] -> 0 | x :: xs -> x + sum xs overflow the stack on a huge list?
The recursive call is not in tail position
Lists in OCaml have a fixed maximum length
Pattern matching allocates on the stack
OCaml does not support recursion on lists
The addition runs after sum xs returns, so every call needs a stack frame. An accumulator version makes the call a tail call.
What happens if you define a recursive OCaml function with let instead of let rec?
The inner call uses an earlier binding of the name, or is unbound
The compiler adds rec automatically when it sees a self call
The function runs only once and then returns its argument unchanged
The function silently becomes tail-recursive and runs faster
Without rec, the name is not in scope inside its own definition, so you get Unbound value or silently use an older definition.
In OCaml, with let p = {x = 1; y = 2}, what does {p with x = 5} do?
Returns a new record with x = 5 and y = 2, leaving p unchanged
Changes the x field of p to 5 in place and returns unit
Returns only the x field of p, now set to the value 5
Fails to compile because record fields can never be changed at all
Functional update copies the record with the listed fields replaced. Records are immutable unless fields are declared mutable.
In OCaml, with type t = {x : int} and p : t, what happens with p.x <- 3?
A compile error, since the field x is not mutable
p.x becomes 3 in place, mutating the record
A new record is returned with x = 3 and p unchanged
A runtime exception is raised on the assignment
Only fields declared mutable, as in {mutable x : int}, can be assigned with <-.
In OCaml, what does let r = ref 0 in r := !r + 1; !r evaluate to?
true
A type error
:= assigns a new value to the reference and ! reads its current contents, so the final !r is 1. Boolean negation in OCaml is not, not !.
In OCaml, what does let a = [|1; 2; 3|] in a.(0) <- 10; a.(0) evaluate to?
Arrays are mutable in OCaml, unlike lists. a.(i) <- v updates an element in place.
What is the type of the expression [1, 2] in OCaml?
(int * int) list
int list
int * int list
(int, int) list
Commas build tuples, so this is a one-element list containing the pair (1, 2). List elements are separated by semicolons.
Compared with ordinary OCaml variants, what is special about polymorphic variants?
They need no prior type declaration and a tag can belong to many types
They can only hold values of type int as their payload
They are checked at runtime instead of at compile time by the type checker
They cannot be used in pattern matching or function arguments
Polymorphic variant tags exist independently of any type definition, so different functions can share and extend sets of tags.
In an OCaml polymorphic variant type written [> ...], what does the > mean?
The type contains at least the listed tags and possibly more
The type contains at most the listed tags and possibly fewer
The type contains exactly the listed tags and nothing else
The listed tags are sorted in descending order by their hash value
> marks an open type with a lower bound on tags; < marks an upper bound, and no sign means exactly those tags.
elixir: What does [1, 2, 3] |> Enum.map(&(&1 * 2)) |> Enum.sum() return in Elixir?
The list is doubled to [2, 4, 6] and then summed. Each |> passes the previous result to the next call.
In Elixir, x |> f(y) is equivalent to which call?
f(x, y)
f(y, x)
x.f(y)
The pipe operator inserts the left value as the first argument of the function on the right.
What happens in Elixir when you evaluate {:ok, v} = {:error, "timeout"}?
A MatchError is raised
v is bound to "timeout"
v is bound to nil
It returns false
= is the match operator. The atoms :ok and :error differ, so the patterns cannot match.
In Elixir, after [h | t] = [1, 2, 3], what is t?
The cons pattern splits a list into its head (1) and its tail, which is the remaining list.
In Elixir, after x = 1, what happens when you evaluate ^x = 2?
A MatchError is raised
x is rebound to the value 2
It returns false
x becomes [1, 2]
The pin operator ^ uses the existing value of x instead of rebinding it, so the match becomes 1 = 2, which fails.
In Elixir, what does f.() return after x = 1; f = fn -> x end; x = 2?
The value 1
The value 2
The value nil
A CompileError
Data is immutable and closures capture the value bound when they are created. Rebinding x later creates a new binding.
What is an Elixir process?
A lightweight BEAM process with its own heap, communicating by messages
An operating system thread that shares memory with other threads
A separate operating system process started for each function call
A green thread that runs on a single heap shared with every other thread
BEAM processes are cheap and isolated; they share nothing and interact only by sending messages, which makes millions of them practical.
In Elixir, what does send(self(), {:hi, 5}); receive do {:hi, n} -> n end return?
The integer 5
The tuple {:hi, 5}
The atom :ok
Nothing, it blocks
The message is already in the process mailbox, so receive matches it and returns n.
In Elixir, what does receive do {:ok, v} -> v end do when no matching message ever arrives and there is no after clause?
It waits indefinitely for a match
It returns nil immediately
It raises after 5 seconds
It returns :timeout after 1 second
Without an after clause, receive blocks until a matching message arrives. Add after 1000 -> :timeout to bound the wait.
What is the difference between GenServer.call and GenServer.cast in Elixir?
call waits for a reply; cast sends a request without waiting
call runs in a new process; cast runs in the caller
call is for reads only; cast is for writes only
call skips the mailbox; cast puts messages in it
call is synchronous and handled by handle_call/3, while cast is asynchronous and handled by handle_cast/2.
Which return value from an Elixir handle_call/3 callback replies to the caller and updates the state?
{:reply, value, new_state}
{:ok, value, new_state}
{:noreply, value}
{:reply, new_state}
{:reply, reply, new_state} sends reply to the caller and keeps new_state as the server state.
In Elixir, what happens by default when GenServer.call gets no reply within 5 seconds?
The calling process exits with a timeout
The call returns nil to the calling process
The call is retried once with a longer timeout
The server process is restarted by its supervisor
The default call timeout is 5000 ms. On timeout the caller exits unless the exit is caught, and the server is not affected.
Under an Elixir Supervisor with the :one_for_one strategy, what happens when one child crashes?
Only that child is restarted
All children are restarted
The supervisor itself stops
The child is removed for good
:one_for_one restarts just the failed child. :one_for_all restarts all of them.
Under an Elixir Supervisor with the :rest_for_one strategy, what happens when a child crashes?
That child and the children started after it are restarted
Only the children started before it are restarted
Every child under the supervisor is restarted at once
Only the crashed child is restarted, the others keep running
:rest_for_one fits when later children depend on earlier ones, so they restart along with the failed one.
What does the "let it crash" approach mean in Elixir and Erlang?
Let a failing process die and have a supervisor restart it cleanly
Wrap every function call in try and rescue so nothing ever fails
Ignore errors and keep running with the corrupted process state in memory
Restart the entire BEAM node and every application on any error
Instead of defensive code everywhere, failures are isolated in processes and supervisors restore a known good state.
In Elixir, what does Process.monitor(pid) give the caller when pid terminates?
A :DOWN message, without crashing the caller
An exit signal that also kills the caller
A return value of :ok from monitor
A restart of pid by the caller
Monitors are one-way and deliver {:DOWN, ref, :process, pid, reason}. Links are two-way and propagate abnormal exits.
What is OTP in the Elixir and Erlang ecosystem?
A set of libraries and behaviours such as GenServer and Supervisor
A web framework for building HTTP servers and real-time apps
The package manager used to install and publish Hex packages
The compiler that turns Elixir source code into BEAM bytecode files
OTP ships with Erlang and provides design principles and tools for building concurrent, fault-tolerant systems.
In Elixir, what does t = Task.async(fn -> 1 + 1 end); Task.await(t) return?
A Task struct
:ok
Task.async runs the function in a new process and Task.await waits for and returns its result (default timeout 5000 ms).
In a Phoenix application, which file maps URL paths to controller actions?
The router, for example lib/my_app_web/router.ex
The endpoint, for example lib/my_app_web/endpoint.ex
The project file mix.exs at the root
The main config file config/config.exs
Routes such as get "/users", UserController, :index live in the router. The endpoint is the entry plug pipeline for every request.
How does Phoenix LiveView keep server-rendered pages interactive?
Through a persistent WebSocket that sends rendered diffs
By shipping the whole app to the browser as client JavaScript
By reloading the full page on every user event
By polling a REST API from a service worker every second
LiveView keeps state on the server in a process and pushes minimal HTML diffs over a WebSocket after each event.
solidity: In Solidity 0.8 or later, with uint8 x = 255, what happens when x + 1 is evaluated outside an unchecked block?
The transaction reverts due to overflow
It wraps around to 0 as in older versions
It becomes 256 in a wider type
It saturates and stays at 255
Since 0.8.0 arithmetic is checked by default and overflow causes a revert with a Panic error.
In Solidity 0.8 or later, with uint8 x = 255, what is the result of x + 1 inside an unchecked { } block?
It wraps to 0
It becomes 256
It stays at 255
It reverts
unchecked disables overflow checks, so the value wraps modulo 2^8. It saves gas but only when overflow is impossible or intended.
In Solidity, which data location is read-only and used for arguments of external functions?
calldata
memory
storage
stack
calldata is the immutable input of the call. It avoids copying arguments into memory, which saves gas.
In Solidity, items is a storage array of structs. What does Item storage it = items[0]; it.x = 5; do?
Changes items[0].x in contract storage
Changes only a temporary copy in memory
Fails to compile without a memory keyword
Changes the value only for this transaction
A storage local is a reference to the state variable. Declaring it as memory would copy the struct, and the change would be lost.
Which of these common EVM operations usually costs the most gas?
Writing a nonzero value to an unused storage slot
Adding two uint256 values on the stack
Reading a function argument from calldata
Emitting an event with one indexed topic and data
Setting a zero storage slot to a nonzero value is one of the most expensive operations, far above arithmetic, calldata reads or logs.
Which Solidity state variable order uses the fewest 32-byte storage slots?
uint128 a; uint128 c; uint256 b;
uint128 a; uint256 b; uint128 c;
uint256 b; uint128 a; uint256 d;
uint128 a; uint256 b; uint256 c;
Adjacent variables are packed into one slot when they fit. Two uint128 values share a slot, so the first order uses 2 slots instead of 3.
Why mark a Solidity state variable that is set once in the constructor as immutable?
Its value is placed in the contract bytecode, so reads avoid storage
It encrypts the value so that other accounts cannot read it
It lets the owner change the value later through a setter
It moves the value into calldata so that it is passed along with each call
immutable values are embedded in the deployed code, so reading them is much cheaper than an SLOAD. They are still publicly visible.
What does the checks-effects-interactions pattern in Solidity recommend?
Update contract state before making external calls
Make external calls before checking inputs
Emit events before validating msg.sender
Avoid require statements in public and external functions
Validate first, then change state, then interact. A reentrant call then sees the already updated state.
A withdraw function sends ETH with msg.sender.call{value: bal}("") and only then sets balances[msg.sender] = 0. What is the fix?
Set the balance to 0 before the external call
Send the ETH twice to confirm the payment
Replace msg.sender with tx.origin in the call
Mark the function as view to block state changes
The attacker's fallback can call withdraw again while the balance is still nonzero. Zeroing first (or a reentrancy guard) blocks this.
What does the nonReentrant modifier from OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard do?
Reverts if a guarded function is re-entered before the first call ends
Limits each address to one call per block to stop repeated calls
Blocks calls from any contract address, allowing only wallets
Refunds all unused gas to the original caller once the function finishes
It sets a status flag on entry and clears it on exit, so a nested call into any nonReentrant function reverts.
Before contract C can move Alice's ERC-20 tokens with transferFrom, what must happen?
Alice calls approve(C, amount) on the token contract
C calls approve(Alice, amount) on the token contract
Alice sends the tokens to C with transfer first
C calls allowance(Alice, C) to unlock them
approve sets an allowance for a spender, and transferFrom spends from it. allowance only reads the current value.
For an ERC-20 token whose decimals() returns 18, how is a balance of 1 whole token stored?
As 10^18 base units
As 18 base units
As 1 base unit
As a float 1.0
Solidity has no floats. decimals only tells wallets how to display the integer amount, so 1 token is 1 followed by 18 zeros.
What is the main difference between ERC-721 and ERC-20 tokens?
Each ERC-721 token has a unique tokenId and is non-fungible
ERC-721 tokens cannot be transferred after they are minted
ERC-721 tokens always use 18 decimals like most ERC-20 tokens
ERC-721 has no function to look up who owns a given token
ERC-20 units are interchangeable. ERC-721 tracks individual tokens, each with ownerOf(tokenId).
In a Solidity modifier, what does the _; statement mean?
The point where the body of the modified function runs
The end of the contract's storage layout for the modifier
A wildcard that matches any function name in the contract
A placeholder for the default return value of the function
Code before _; runs first, then the function body, then any code after _;.

The call reverts with the message "not owner"
The function runs but returns no value
The call succeeds and logs a warning
The function runs with the owner's address
require reverts the whole call and undoes its state changes when the condition is false.
Can a Solidity contract read the events it emitted in earlier transactions?
No, event logs can only be read off-chain
Yes, through the built-in logs array
Yes, but only within the same block
Yes, by calling the event like a function
Logs are stored in transaction receipts, which the EVM cannot access. Store data in state variables if contracts need it.
What does marking a Solidity event parameter as indexed do?
Stores it as a log topic so clients can filter by it
Saves it in contract storage for later contract reads
Makes it hidden from block explorers and wallets
Sorts the emitted events by that parameter value
Indexed parameters become topics that nodes can filter on. A non-anonymous event can have up to 3 indexed parameters.
A Solidity contract has both receive() external payable and fallback() external payable. ETH arrives with empty calldata. Which runs?
Only receive()
Only fallback()
Both, receive first
Neither; it reverts
receive handles plain ETH transfers with empty calldata. fallback runs when calldata matches no function, or when receive is absent.
A call to a Solidity contract has calldata that matches none of its function selectors. Which function runs?
fallback(), if the contract defines one
receive(), if the contract defines one
The constructor, run once more
The first public function in the file
fallback is the catch-all for unknown selectors. Without it, the call reverts.
Why is require(tx.origin == owner) discouraged for authorization in Solidity?
A malicious contract the owner interacts with can pass the check
tx.origin is not available in contracts after Solidity 0.8
tx.origin costs more gas than any other authorization check
tx.origin is always the zero address when called through another contract
tx.origin is the account that started the transaction, even through other contracts. Use msg.sender, the immediate caller.
